column3: Directly parallels the angelic reassurance and announcement of a learned son.
Its divine-names theme supports the significance of Yahya's assigned name, though not its unprecedented status.
Shares the glad-tidings root but concerns believers' joy at revelation, not a child's announcement.
Closely parallels the divine good news of a son, with the boy's defining quality supplied.
The same challenge about a prior namesake directly clarifies the focus verse's unique-name claim.
Offers a contrasting human reception of birth news, highlighting the positive force of Zakariyya's glad tidings.
The creating verb and pronoun do not illuminate the birth announcement or naming.
Immediately supplies Zakariyya's fear of succession and his request for an heir that the focus answers.
Another divinely announced figure receives a specified future name, paralleling named prophetic good news.
The earth's gathering function has no meaningful connection to the focus reading.
Its appeal to creation from nothing supports the divine possibility underlying the elderly couple's new child.
Mentioning God's name over lawful food concerns ritual authorization, not naming a child.
A close parallel: angels announce a child to Mary and specify his name and future stature.
A request for judgment and righteous company only remotely parallels a request for a divinely granted heir.
It uses glad tidings for future mercy and gardens rather than a named child.
The earth as a resting place does not support the focus themes.
Direct continuation of Zakariyya's request, defining the hoped-for heir and his righteousness.
Praise of the Lord's name is a separate devotional use of naming.
Explicitly recounts the answer to Zakariyya: Yahya is given and his wife's condition restored.
Introduces the account as the Lord's mercy to Zakariyya, framing the announcement that follows.
The prohibition on insulting labels offers only a distant contrast to divinely assigning Yahya's name.
Its lack of shelter has no bearing on the focus verse.
Named worship in elevated houses is a distinct use of the name motif.
Praise of God's great name does not illuminate the child's distinctive name.
Directly parallels fear being answered with reassurance and the good news of a learned son.
Immediate response to the announcement, voicing the biological obstacle of age and barrenness.
The ironic command to announce punishment is a contrastive use of good-news language.
Mary's question about receiving a son parallels Zakariyya's astonishment at miraculous conception.
Immediate divine answer grounds the announced birth in creation from prior nonexistence.
God's name in protected places of worship is not materially connected to Yahya's naming.
Calling on the Merciful offers a broad devotional backdrop but no focused birth or naming link.
God's beautiful names and creating activity provide a broad theological counterpart to assigned identity.
The invocation at a letter's opening is another naming practice, not a parallel to the child's name.
The mention of messengers and Moses' speech provides no specific support for the focus.
Continues the description of Yahya's divinely granted qualities after his announced birth.
The ironic announcement of punishment is contrastive evidence about the verb, not support for the birth scene.
The rhetorical refusal to equate unlike people only distantly echoes the focus's denial of a namesake.
Divine command bringing a matter into being supports miraculous birth, though this verse concerns Jesus.
Naming a spring is a remote lexical parallel without the focus's identity or birth themes.
The contrast of neither dying nor living does not illuminate Yahya's announcement.
Its humility before the Messenger is unrelated to the child's name or miraculous birth.
Defines a messenger as bearer of good news and warning, a broad framing for the announcement language.
Its punishment formula only shares wording with an unrelated candidate and has no focus link.
Completes Yahya's early portrait with peace across birth, death, and resurrection.
Uses glad tidings for the believers' final reward, not a child or named vocation.
The protection of orphan boys' future inheritance is only distantly analogous to household continuity.
Begins Zakariyya's private prayer that culminates in the announced son.
God's name over sacrificial provision is a distinct ritual context.
Prior family fear supplies no specific relation to Zakariyya's petition or answer.
A named term marks cosmic duration, only remotely related to a uniquely assigned personal name.
A general command to give believers glad tidings lacks the focus's birth and naming content.
The confession of neglecting prayer is unrelated to the focus.
Zakariyya's aged weakness immediately establishes the impossibility that makes the announced son a mercy.
The ironic good news of punishment is contrastive use of the same announcement formula.
Mention of God's name in mosques concerns worship-space protection, not Yahya's name.
Immediate sequel: Zakariyya requests and receives a sign confirming the announcement.
Remembrance of the Lord's name is a separate devotional practice.
Rejection of revelation and comparison with Moses do not bear on the focus.
Zakariyya's prayer not to be left alone is the direct petition answered by Yahya's gift.
A messenger as bearer of good news and warning is a broad, non-natal parallel.
Its warning about faith after decisive signs does not clarify the announcement.
Direct continuation: the announced child is addressed by name and given wisdom while young.
A second named prophetic child is announced as glad tidings, closely paralleling Yahya's vocation.
The reference to Adam "before" does not establish a useful link to the unique-name statement.
Continues the immediate narrative with Zakariyya's confirming sign and worshipful instruction.
The communal designation "Muslims" is a different kind of naming from Yahya's singular name.
Divine response to Noah's call broadly resembles answered prayer but lacks the heir and birth themes.
Calling from behind rooms has no meaningful connection to the focus.
The Prophet's general office as bearer of good news provides only a broad lexical parallel.
Angels announce Yahya by name to Zakariyya while he prays, the closest parallel account.
Direct continuation describing Yahya's filial goodness and freedom from rebellion.
God's uniquely beautiful names give a theological backdrop for the focus's distinctive-name language.
The messenger announces to Mary the gift of a pure son, closely paralleling 19:7's announcement.
The disappearance of former generations supplies at most a distant contrast to a name without precedent.
A named cosmic term is only a remote analogy to assigning an unprecedented personal name.
The question about prior messengers and deities does not illuminate Yahya's birth or name.
Naming God over food is a different ritual application of the name motif.
God's teaching of names supports naming as meaningful knowledge, but not the focus's familial announcement.
Lists Zakariyya and Yahya together among the righteous, confirming their prophetic association.
The destruction of earlier prosperous generations is unrelated to the birth announcement.
The messenger's good-news-and-warning role gives a broad framework for divine announcing language.
Human creation and endowment of hearing and sight only broadly supports divine creative power.
The sky's splitting has no connection to the focus reading.
General prophetic good news and warning lacks the focus's named-child content.
A barren-age birth announcement to Abraham's wife closely parallels the miraculous good news to Zakariyya.
God's increase of guidance is unrelated to the announced son and unique name.
The command to give believers good news is not a parallel to the personal birth announcement.
Mountains joining David in praise do not illuminate the focus.
Rules about food named for God remain a separate ritual use of the name motif.
The ironic announcement of punishment is contrastive rather than positive support.
A named contractual term and written debt are unrelated to the child's name or birth.
Glad tidings of victory and divine help are a broad, non-natal parallel.
The example of prophets' unfaithful wives does not bear on the focus's miraculous family gift.
Remembering the Lord's name in prayer is a distinct devotional theme.
The declaration of disavowal has no relevance to the focus.
Pilgrimage regulations do not illuminate the announced birth or naming.
God's creative command over the cosmos gives only very general support for divine power.
Provision from heaven and divine signs are only a broad backdrop to God's gift of a son.
Household etiquette around the Prophet does not bear on Yahya's announcement.
The question for a healer has no meaningful connection to the focus.
Mary's birth, naming, and entrustment introduce the sanctuary context from which Zakariyya's own request arises.
Zakariyya's encounter with Mary's provision directly precedes and motivates his prayer for offspring.
His immediate prayer for good offspring is answered by the announcement of Yahya in 3:39 and parallels 19:7.
Zakariyya asks how he can have a son in old age with a barren wife, directly mirroring 19:8.
His request for a confirming sign parallels the sign granted in the immediate continuation of 19:7.
God's creation by command answers Mary's question about a child and supports the miraculous-birth logic of the focus.
The comparison of Jesus to Adam offers a broad creation-by-command ground for exceptional birth.
Sarah's astonishment at bearing a child while old and barren is a close parallel to Zakariyya's response.
Abraham praises God for granting Ishmael and Isaac in old age, directly paralleling a divinely granted late-life son.
The recipient questions a son's good news after old age has touched him, closely paralleling Zakariyya's astonishment.
The angels insist that their good news is true and forbid despair, clarifying the authority of a miraculous announcement.
The divine explanation of Mary's miraculous son as an easy act and a sign closely parallels the logic supplied to Zakariyya.
Mary's preserved chastity and the divine breathing of spirit provide a second major Qur'anic instance of extraordinary conception.
Abraham's prayer for a righteous child directly precedes his receipt of good news of a son.
Sarah reacts to the announced son by stressing her old age and barrenness, a direct analogue to Zakariyya's situation.
The angels confirm the announcement as the decree of the Wise, Knowing Lord, reinforcing divine authority behind such news.
The later account of Mary conceiving by divine spirit provides a concise parallel for miraculous birth.
